analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited soft money to national political parties and forces disclosure of campaign-season TV attack ads.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 240-189 and the Senate 60-40, and President Bush signed it into law on March 27, 2002.
analysis.plain_summary: This law cuts off the unlimited, unregulated "soft money" that national political parties used to collect from corporations, unions, and big donors. It also requires anyone who airs a TV or radio ad mentioning a federal candidate in the weeks before an election to disclose who paid for it, and bans corporate and union treasury money for those ads. It raises other contribution limits and strengthens disclosure, penalties, and the foreign-money ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who learn who is paying for campaign ads and see parties and candidates cut off from unlimited, unreported donations; candidates and parties must raise money under limits that are publicly reported.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to see who pays for ads

how_it_helps.text: National party committees are barred from soliciting or spending money that is not subject to federal contribution limits, reporting, and prohibitions — the unlimited "soft money" channel — and federal candidates and officeholders are barred from raising it [S3][S4].

Any person who spends more than $10,000 a year on broadcast, cable, or satellite ads that refer to a federal candidate within 60 days of a general election or 30 days of a primary must file a disclosure naming the spender and major funders within 24 hours [S3][S4].
Corporations and unions are barred from paying for those electioneering communications out of their treasury funds [S4].

Donations of $200 or more to a presidential inaugural committee must be disclosed, foreign nationals are banned from giving to it, and the ban on foreign money in elections is extended to independent expenditures and electioneering communications [S2][S4].

Fundraising on federal property is extended to state and local elections and to soft money, and candidates must appear on screen and state they approve their own ads to keep the lowest broadcast rate [S3][S4].
Criminal penalties for knowing violations are raised, the statute of limitations is extended from three to five years, and all FEC filings must be posted on the internet within 48 hours [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: National party committees lose the unlimited soft-money stream; corporations and unions lose the ability to fund candidate-focused ads from their general treasuries; large donors gain higher hard-money limits but face the same disclosure rules.

drawbacks.text: The law raises the individual contribution limit from $1,000 to $2,000 per candidate, lifts aggregate limits to $37,500-$57,500, and indexes them to inflation, letting bigger donors give more even as soft money is cut off [S4].

State and local party committees may still spend limited amounts of non-federal money on some voter-registration and get-out-the-vote activity, with a $10,000-per-donor annual cap, so a regulated soft-money channel remains at the state level [S3].

The 40 senators who voted no argued the restrictions on broadcast ads that mention candidates in the weeks before elections restrict political speech — an objection courts later weighed in litigation over the law [S10].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: unlimited, unreported party money and unattributed campaign-season ads end, in exchange for higher caps on disclosed individual donations and some remaining state-party soft money with a $10,000 donor cap. On balance the disclosure and soft-money ban outweigh the higher limits, though the law did not stop money from moving to outside groups over time.

outcome.mechanism: It squeaked through the House only after supporters collected 218 discharge-petition signatures to force a floor vote, passed 240-189, cleared the Senate 60-40 after a 68-32 cloture vote, and was signed by President Bush on March 27, 2002.

narrative.text: The bill was reported adversely by the House Administration Committee but the other committees were discharged and it was placed on the Union Calendar on July 10, 2001 [S7].
The first House rule for debate failed on July 12, 2001; the bill only reached the floor after a discharge petition by Mr. Turner received the requisite 218 signatures in January 2002 [S7].

Substitute amendments by Reps. Armey and Ney, which would have replaced the bill, were debated but the Shays version prevailed; the House passed it 240-189 on February 14, 2002, with Democrats voting 198-12 yes and Republicans 41-176 [S7][S8].
The Senate invoked cloture 68-32 (all 50 Democrats yes, 32 Republicans no) and passed the bill without amendment 60-40 (48 of 50 Democrats yes, 11 of 49 Republicans yes) on March 20, 2002 [S9][S10].
The President signed it on March 27, 2002, and it became Public Law 107-155 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary voters gained disclosure of campaign ad funders and the end of unlimited soft money to national parties; national party committees, corporate and union treasuries, and opponents of campaign-disclosure requirements lost the fight.

sides.party_line_note: The bill carried a bipartisan name and some cross-party support, but the vote broke heavily by party: in the House 198 of 211 voting Democrats backed it against 41 of 222 Republicans (240-189), and in the Senate 48 of 50 Democrats backed it against 11 of 49 Republicans (60-40).

industries.note: The law bars national party committees from soliciting or spending unlimited, unregulated soft money, closing the channel that let big donors and corporations give beyond federal limits [S3][S4]. Their loss is the public's gain in disclosure and contribution limits.
Corporations and unions can no longer pay for broadcast ads that name a federal candidate in the run-up to an election from their general treasury funds [S4].

Stations must keep and open for inspection records of political ad purchase requests and air sponsorship identification statements, adding compliance work, while campaign advertising itself remains a revenue source [S4][S5].
The per-candidate limit doubles to $2,000 and aggregate limits rise to $37,500-$57,500 with inflation indexing, increasing how much the biggest donors can legally give even as soft money ends [S4].
